Seven months building a tool that catches API contract drift. Not writing specs. Checking whether the API you ship still matches the contract you published.
I ran it against 98 endpoints. 12 contracts. My own workspace.

It isn't. Barely any of it is a break. It's small stuff piling up. Nobody decides to do it.

memberCount declared as a number. API returning a string. Nothing crashed. Tests passed. A strict client would break.
pathname promised in the response. Not there. Sometimes there, sometimes not. Spec never updated when it became conditional.

articles.author: Philip D'Souza
articles.description:
ChatGPT is good at reasoning over health data and cannot reach Apple Health on its own. It does not speak MCP, so it cannot call a local tool the way Cursor or Claude can. A webhook bridge fixes that, and the key design choice is whose endpoint receives the data.
The flow is one direction: your iPhone POSTs structured JSON to a URL you configure, and you feed that into ChatGPT. The app never sends your data to a server run by the developer. The payload is clean and typed: every metric has a stable lower-case name, an explicit unit, and dates with a UTC offset, so the model never guesses. The same names the MCP server returns.
Three ways to wire it up, from zero code to fully automated: export to a file and drag it into ChatGPT, stand up a fifteen-line local FastAPI receiver on your LAN, or use n8n or Home Assistant if you already run them. Then the privacy distinction. The MCP path keeps the data on your machine with zero network traffic. The webhook path adds a second hop, from your endpoint to OpenAI, and that hop is when the data leaves your control. Use MCP when your agent supports it, the webhook when you specifically want ChatGPT's reasoning.
Full guide, with the real payload, the FastAPI receiver, and a full ChatGPT walkthrough: https://dub.sh/hBVeLDr
articles.title: Connect Apple Health to ChatGPT via webhook: your data, their agent

articles.author: Richa Singh
articles.description:
An ERP can produce incorrect inventory even when every individual API appears to work correctly. The failure usually happens when two users, integrations, or background workers attempt to reserve the same stock at nearly the same time. A typical example is an order service reading available_quantity = 10, processing an order for 7 units, while another request reads the same value before either transaction commits.
This is an architecture problem, not simply an API bug. Good ERP Development Services must define transaction boundaries, concurrency rules, idempotency, and observability before scaling the application.
For teams building a custom ERP, this architecture pattern can be implemented with Node.js, PostgreSQL, Docker, and AWS. Organizations evaluating custom ERP development services …
